title: Dollars and Change
big_idea: Coins and notes make an amount in different ways, and change is what we count up
child_idea: Every coin and note has a value. We count the biggest first. Change is the money we count up from the price to the money we paid.

topics: Counting money in cents up to $1 and in dollars up to $100 (Primary 1, p. 31)
Making an amount in different ways, and change (Primary 1, p. 31)
Money written with a decimal point, such as $1.50, is Primary 2 (p. 33): not used
moe.note: Strand label for the tutor only. BEYOND PRIMARY 1 ON PURPOSE at Think harder and Go further only. Start here is Primary 1 work (school papers set it in the last term of the year): count mixed coins to 100 cents and notes within $30, swap a coin for coins of the same value, circle coins that make an amount, compare a note with a coin, and find change from $5 by counting up. Think harder is Primary 1 level with larger amounts: two things and change from $10, the price found from the money paid and the change given (working backwards), a one-dollar coin and change in cents ($1 is 100 cents, a Primary 1 story), and comparing sets of coins. Go further is beyond Primary 1: the fewest notes and coins for $73 and for a change of $13 (school papers set the fewest-pieces question for smaller amounts; the notes $10 and $50 and the amount $73 are the stretch), how many different amounts three pieces can make (listing every case is not a syllabus item), and a shop with several things bought for one dollar. Think harder T2 (all the ways to make 50 cents with 10 cent and 20 cent coins, 3 ways) is a listing puzzle, also beyond the syllabus. Owner decision, 22 and 23 Oct 2026: strong content with scaffolding, said plainly to families; every lesson names a beyond item. Do not describe the lesson as MOE-aligned. Money notation follows the Primary 1 papers (23 Oct): cents as 50¢ (never 50c), dollars as $5, never $1.50, and no amount that mixes dollars and cents; the only mix is a $1 = 100 cent conversion with the answer in cents. Coins: 5, 10, 20, 50 cents and $1; notes: $2, $5, $10, $50. There is no $20 note, so the fewest notes and coins for $73 is 5 ($50, $10, $10, $2, $1). The play money is stylised and marked PLAY MONEY; it does not copy any real note or coin. Owner decision D1 (the rules on notes and coins) is open before the first printing. Contest tag (tutor only): all the ways, fewest pieces, how many different amounts.

contest_moves: all the ways to make an amount
work backwards: paid and change given, find the price
contest_where: Think harder, Go further and the Investigation
objectives: Name the coins (5¢, 10¢, 20¢, 50¢, $1) and notes ($2, $5, $10, $50) by their value, and count a handful of mixed coins or notes, biggest first.
Make the same amount in different ways, and swap a coin for coins of the same value ($1 is 100¢).
Find change by counting up from the price to the money paid.
Think harder: pay for two things, find change from a $1 coin in cents, list every way to make 50¢ with two kinds of coin, and compare sets of coins.
Go further: the fewest notes and coins for an amount, how many different amounts a few pieces can make, and a small shop.

remember: Count in 5s and 10s to 100 (Term 1 Lesson 4, taught again with a number row)
Put four coins in order from least to most, by the number on each coin (taught again with the kit coins)
Count up from one number to another to find the gap (Term 1 Lesson 7, taught again on a line)

Nothing from the lessons before is needed: the warm-up counts in 5s and 10s with a number row, puts four coins in order, and counts up on a line. The words value, change and count up are taught in Explore and the Mini-lesson.

A child who misses it watches the recording, does workbook pages 1 and 2 and cuts out the play-money pages before the next lesson. A child who joins here cold can follow: the warm-up counts in 5s and 10s again and Start here keeps to coins within 100 cents and notes within $30.

child: Your Term 3 workbook, pages 1 to 5, and the two play-money pages (pages 6 and 7), already cut out by a grown-up: 16 coins and 13 notes
The $1 tokens from Term 2 Lesson 10: they are the $1 coins. If the tokens are lost, use 5 counters or buttons
No printer or no cutting? Small pieces of paper with the value written on each one
A pencil, a rubber and spare paper

kit_pages: Play money, coins (page 6): 4 five-cent, 6 ten-cent, 4 twenty-cent and 2 fifty-cent coins. Play money, notes (page 7): 5 two-dollar, 4 five-dollar, 3 ten-dollar and 1 fifty-dollar note. 29 pieces in all, cut out by a grown-up. The $1 coins are the tokens from Term 2 Lesson 10. Keep the money in an envelope: it comes back in the next two lessons and in Mi's Challenge Quest.
materials.notes: No ruler is needed. Nothing needs to be bought. The money is PLAY MONEY, not real: it is stylised and marked, and it is not a copy of any real note or coin. Small pieces stay on the table: nothing goes in the mouth or ears; keep them away from younger brothers and sisters. Real coins only if a grown-up is present. No matches, toothpicks or anything sharp. Nobody cuts during the lesson: a grown-up cuts the pieces beforehand.

timing.notes: Opening is 2 minutes (the routine and rules were taught in the first lesson of Term 1). Explore has 11 minutes with the play money: make 60 cents two ways, count two handfuls, and give change twice. The mini-lesson has 11: the value on each piece, count the biggest first, a dollar is 100 cents, change by counting up, and a try. The workbook has 32 minutes: Start here takes a middle child about 17 minutes, so pages 3 to 5 are for home for most children. The last 5 minutes are the standing buffer; the optional Go further slide is used only if the lesson is on time.

slides.title: Dollars and Change

blocks.head: TODAY WE WILL
items: Count coins and notes, and give change.

slides.note: Lesson 4 of Term 3, 90 minutes. Objective: name coins and notes by value, count mixed coins and notes biggest first, make one amount in different ways, and find change by counting up. Plain statement for families: counting coins and notes and change from $5 or $10 is Primary 1 work; listing every way to make an amount, the fewest notes and coins for $73 and how many different amounts three pieces can make go past the school Primary 1 syllabus on purpose. Time plan: opening 0 to 2, warm-up 2 to 8, sneak-peek 8 to 12, explore 12 to 23, mini-lesson 23 to 34, brain break 34 to 38, workbook 38 to 70, talk 70 to 76, exit ticket 76 to 82, look-back 82 to 85, flex time and goodbye 85 to 90 (the buffer: do not start anything new). Think harder, Go further and the Investigation are for every child to choose. Say the recording notice in one line: you and the screen only; a child may keep the camera off.
slides.subtitle: Coins, notes and change

mascot.say: Hi, I'm Mi. Let's notice, test and explain why!

slides.title: Warm-up: count in 5s and 10s

blocks.text: Clap on every 10.

slides.note: Count in 5s to 100 with a clap on each 10, then in 10s to 100. This is Term 1 Lesson 4 taught again, and it is the counting that every coin needs. A child who has not counted in 5s counts along the number row on the slide: they hear it before they say it. Ask: how many 5s make 100? Do not ask for it; just count together twice. No writing, no marks.

slides.title: Put the coins in order

blocks.text: Read the number on each coin. Put your coins in order. Least first.

slides.note: Four coins on the slide: 20, 5, 50 and 10 cents. Children take the same four coins from their kit and put them in a row from least to most, reading the number on each coin. Ask: which coin is worth the least (5¢); which is worth the most (50¢); what is the order (5¢, 10¢, 20¢, 50¢). Say the cent sign: the number tells the value. A child with no kit coins writes the four numbers on paper and puts them in order. No writing is needed, no marks.

slides.title: Count up on a line

blocks.text: Count up from 28 to 35. How many steps?

slides.note: Counting up to find a gap (Term 1 Lesson 7, taught again). Count up from 28 to 35 with a finger on the line: 29, 30, ..., 35, which is 7 steps. Then ask: from 46 to 50 (4 steps). Children answer aloud. Say: change works the same way, we count up from the price to the money we paid. A child who is unsure counts the ticks aloud with a finger on the screen. No writing.

slides.title: Sneak-peek puzzles

blocks.text: Ideas we have not learnt yet. A guess is a great start. Nobody is marked.

cols.head: PUZZLE 1: anyone can try
items: Count the coins. How many cents? Write the number.

cols.head: PUZZLE 2: think
items: Does Mei have more money than Ben? Circle Yes or No. I know because ___.

slides.note: Puzzle 1 (3 ten-cent coins and 2 five-cent coins: 40 cents) is an access question: any child can count in 10s then 5s, or add on. Puzzle 2 is a thinking question on the lesson idea: 10 ten-cent coins make 100 cents, and a one-dollar coin is 100 cents, so they have the same. Say: two sneak-peek puzzles, ideas we have not learnt yet; a guess is a great start and I do not know is welcome; nobody is marked. Children write on their own paper. Nobody holds paper to the camera. There is no private chat. Answers: 40 cents; No, the same. Do not reveal puzzle 2 until Talk time. Do not write scores or keep a list.

slides.title: Explore: make 60¢

blocks.text: Same money. Different coins.

slides.note: Round 1, about 4 minutes. Children use the coins from their kit (5, 10, 20 and 50 cents). Look at the number on each coin; the number is the value. Make 60 cents: one way (for example 50 and 10), then a different way (20, 20 and 20; or six 10-cent coins; or 20, 20, 10 and 10). Take volunteers: tell me one way. The same amount can be made from different coins. A child who finds only one way is asked: can you use only 10-cent coins? The slide shows no answer. A child with no coins writes the values on paper. Do not name a child with a wrong answer.

slides.title: Explore: count the money

blocks.text: Start with the biggest coin. Count on.

slides.note: Round 2, about 3 minutes, main room. Children count the money in each picture aloud, starting with the biggest coin, and may put the same coins on the table. Picture A is 50, 60, 70 (70 cents). Picture B is 20, 40, 60, 65 (65 cents). Ask: how many cents is picture A; how many is picture B. The totals are never on the slide. A child who counts each coin as 1 (3 coins) is asked: what is the number on the coin?

slides.title: Explore: change

items: A sweet costs 40¢. You pay with a 50¢ coin.
A ruler costs $6. You pay with a $10 note.
Count up from the price to the money you paid.

slides.note: Round 3, about 3 minutes. Change is the money the shop gives back. We count up from the price to the money we paid, putting down a coin or note at each step. Start at 40 cents and put down coins until you reach 50 cents: a 10-cent coin is the change. Then the ruler: start at $6 and put down two-dollar notes or dollar tokens until you reach $10 (two $2 notes, or four $1 tokens): the change is $4. Ask: how much change for the sweet (10 cents); for the ruler ($4). The tags show the prices only; the changes are never on the slide.

slides.title: Coins and notes

blocks.text: Read the number. The number is the value.

slides.note: Name the pieces: coins are 5, 10, 20 and 50 cents and 1 dollar; notes are 2, 5, 10 and 50 dollars. Say it both ways: fifty-cent coin and 50¢; five-dollar note and $5. We write cents with the cent sign after the number (50¢) and dollars with the dollar sign before it ($5). We never mix them in one amount. The value is the number on the piece, not its size. These are PLAY MONEY: stylised and marked, not real. Ask: which piece is worth the most (the $50 note); which coin is worth the least (5¢).

slides.title: Count the biggest first

blocks.text: Biggest first. Then count on.

slides.note: Worked example: a 50-cent coin, two 10-cent coins and a 5-cent coin. Start with the biggest, 50, then count on: 60, 70, 75. The total is 75 cents. Touch each coin as you say its count. Counting the biggest first is quicker and easier to keep track of than counting in any order. Children count along with you. Say: the answer is 75¢, with the cent sign.

slides.title: A dollar is 100¢
slides.note: One dollar is the same as 100 cents. Two 50-cent coins make 100 cents. Ten 10-cent coins make 100 cents: count in tens to 100 with the children on their fingers (the kit has six 10-cent coins, so nobody needs ten); the ten coins and the sentence appear on the answer slide after the children have counted. So a one-dollar coin is worth the same as two fifty-cent coins or ten ten-cent coins. Children check on the table with their own coins: put two 50¢ coins next to a $1 token. A 50-cent coin is worth less than a one-dollar coin even though 50 is more than 1: the dollar sign and the cent sign are different units. Do not write $1.00 or 1.50 anywhere: we never use a decimal point for money in this lesson. The answer slide shows the ten coins: say 'two 50¢ coins make $1, ten 10¢ coins make $1' after the children have counted.

slides.title: Change: count up

blocks.text: The ball costs $8. You pay with a $10 note. How much change?

slides.note: Worked with a question. The ball costs $8 and you pay with a $10 note. Count up from $8 to $10 on the line: $9, $10, which is 2 steps, so the change is $2. Ask first: how much change? Children count up on their fingers or with their coins. Say the answer after they have tried. Change is what the shop gives back: the price plus the change makes the money you paid. A child who subtracts is welcome to: 10 minus 8 is 2.

slides.title: Your turn

cols.head: CHANGE
items: A rubber costs $5. You pay with a $10 note. How much change?

blocks.text: Write both answers on your paper.

slides.note: Two quick items on the children's own paper: count 20, 20 and 5 cents (45 cents), and change for a $5 rubber paid with a $10 note ($5). Walk the cameras and wait 10 seconds before helping. Nobody holds paper up. The next slide shows the answers and children tick their own work. Answers: 45¢; $5.

slides.title: Check: your turn

blocks.text: Count: 45¢. Change: $5.

slides.note: Read both answers aloud so a child watching the recording can tick their own work. 20, 40, 45 gives 45 cents; from $5 count up to $10 gives $5. Never ask a child to show a wrong answer to the group. A child who writes 45 without the cent sign is asked: 45 what? Cents.

slides.title: Coin hop

blocks.text: Stand up. I call an amount.
Hop once for every 5¢ and count out loud: 5, 10, 15 ...
Sip some water.

slides.note: Four minutes. Stand up on camera with a little clear space. Call an amount in cents (20¢, 35¢, 50¢, 10¢) and children hop once for every 5¢, counting aloud in 5s: for 35¢ that is 7 hops. Then call two amounts in a row so children keep counting on from the last number. No equipment, no running; a child may stay seated and tap the table. Do not give prizes or compare children.

slides.title: Workbook page 1: Start here

blocks.text: Questions 1 to 3.
Q1. Count the money. How many cents?
Q2. Count the notes. How many dollars?
Q3. The fifty-cent coin. Count in 10s, then in 5s.

slides.note: Read questions 1 to 3 aloud. Children work on their own with their play money; the tutor walks the cameras and asks how do you know. Wait 10 seconds before helping. After question 3 any child may choose to carry on or try Think harder. Question 1: count the coins, biggest first. Question 2: count the notes. Question 3: a fifty-cent coin is worth the same as how many ten-cent coins, and how many five-cent coins.

slides.title: Check page 1
slides.note: Read each answer aloud. Children tick their own page with a tick. Never ask a child to show a wrong answer to the group. Answers: Q1 80¢; Q2 $19; Q3 5 ten-cent coins and 10 five-cent coins.

slides.title: Workbook page 2: Start here

blocks.text: Questions 4 to 6. Take your time.
Question 4. Circle the coins that make 55¢.
Question 5. Which is worth more: the $2 note or the $1 coin?
Question 6. Ravi buys a toy car for $3. He pays with a five-dollar note. How much change?

slides.note: Read questions 4 to 6 aloud. Question 4: circle the coins that make 55 cents. Question 5: look at a two-dollar note and a one-dollar coin; which is worth more? Question 6: Ravi buys a toy car for $3 and pays with a five-dollar note; how much change? Children may use their play money to check. Wait 10 seconds before helping.

slides.title: Check page 2
slides.note: Read each answer aloud so a child watching the recording can tick their own work. Never ask a child to show a wrong answer to the group. Answers: Q4 the 50¢ coin and one 5¢ coin (55¢); Q5 the $2 note; Q6 $2.

slides.title: Choose your next page

rows: Two things, find the price, every way, sets of coins
The fewest notes and coins, how many amounts
Finish and check your own work

blocks.text: Everyone may choose. Not finished? Pages 3 to 5 are for home too.

slides.note: Invite the whole group at once, for example: when you have finished Start here, you can choose Think harder, Go further or the Investigation. Never announce who is on which page and never name a child. Pairs are not split unless both children agree. Model answers are in the tutor guide. About 5 minutes.

slides.title: Talk and explain

blocks.head: A CHILD SAYS
items: A fifty-cent coin is worth more than a one-dollar coin.

blocks.text: Is the child right? How could we check with our coins?
I think ... because ...

slides.note: One minute of talk to the grown-up next to you, or to your screen. Children test it with their coins: put a $1 token next to two 50¢ coins. Then volunteers first; a pass is always fine; never call a child by name to answer. Model answer: no. A one-dollar coin is 100 cents, and a fifty-cent coin is only 50 cents, half of a dollar. Two fifty-cent coins make a dollar. 50 is a bigger number than 1, but a cent is much smaller than a dollar. Repeat each child answer in your own words for the recording. The child who says it is in another class: no cast name is given the wrong answer.

slides.title: Back to the sneak-peek

blocks.text: Puzzle 1: 40¢. Puzzle 2: No. They have the same: 10 ten-cent coins make 100¢, and $1 is 100¢.

slides.note: Reveal both puzzles now. Say: many of you wrote a good reason. Do not read out anyone earlier answer. Puzzle 1: 3 ten-cent coins and 2 five-cent coins is 30 and 10, which is 40 cents. Puzzle 2: 10 ten-cent coins make 100 cents and a one-dollar coin is 100 cents, so Mei and Ben have the same money. It was the same idea as the child in the talk question.

slides.title: Exit ticket

blocks.text: On your own. No looking back.

slides.note: Children answer on page 5. Read E1, E2 and E3 aloud, and the four options of E2 (the figures on the slide are small). Children tick their own ticket against the next slide. Nobody holds paper to the camera and there is no private chat.

slides.title: Check the exit ticket
slides.note: Read each answer aloud. Children tick their own ticket with a tick. Answers: 90¢; option 3, $6; $15.

slides.title: Look-back
slides.note: Three minutes. Children tick or write the look-back box on page 5. A pass is always allowed. It is never marked, never collected in front of the group and never read out. If a child ticks I am still stuck, a grown-up may photograph that page after class and send it to the business WhatsApp (the number is in the parent summary, never on a slide). You then help in the open session next lesson. Never a direct message to a child. The Next time I will try row is optional.

mascot.say: Take your time. You can pass.

slides.title: Well done, inquirers!

blocks.text: Show a grown-up one thing you found out today.

blocks.head: NEXT LESSON
items: Have ready: the price-tag page, cut out by a grown-up (12 tags), and your play money in its envelope.

slides.note: Say goodbye and thank the grown-ups. Minutes 85 to 90 are flex time: the buffer. If you ran late, finish any open item (the look-back). Do not start anything new. Remind families that the next lesson needs the price-tag page cut out by a grown-up (12 tags) and the play money and $1 tokens in their envelope. If the whole class is ahead, show the optional slides and use the Spare-time menu from the tutor guide.

slides.title: Go further: fewest pieces

blocks.text: Make 85¢ with coins. What is the fewest number of coins?

slides.note: Optional, only if you are on time. The tray shows several of each coin, so the picture does not give the answer. 85 cents with the fewest coins: 50, 20, 10 and 5, which is 4 coins. Many children will try 20 and 20 and 20 and 20 and 5 (5 coins) first. Ask: can anyone beat 5 coins? The biggest coin that fits goes first, then the next biggest that fits. Take two answers and move on. This links to Go further and the Investigation.

slides.title: If we have time: pick one

rows: More coins always means more money? Test it.
Pick 3 coins. Say the total. Ask for the coins.
Show a toy how to count up for change.

blocks.text: Optional. Everyone may join.

slides.note: Optional Spare-time menu, used only if the whole class is ahead. Pick one or two activities (3 to 5 minutes each); full tutor lines and answers are in the tutor guide. Never start new content and never name who is ahead. Slow down with how do you know rather than rushing on. These minutes come from the flex buffer and are not part of the 90-minute sum.

lines.text: @rec
Hello, inquirers! Pencil ready, and your play money on the table. Cameras can be on or off, as you like.
This lesson is recorded so a friend who is away can catch up. The recording has me, the shared screen and any voice that is not muted. You may keep your microphone and camera off.
Microphone off until I ask you to speak. To answer, say it with me on three, show fingers, or give a thumbs up. Nobody holds paper up to the camera.
Today we count coins and notes, and we learn what change is. The money is play money. It is not real, and it stays on the table.
Greet the whole group warmly. Do not use children's first names on the recording.

Keep this to two minutes. Say the recording statement and the microphone routine in the same words every lesson, for anyone who joined late. The routine and the four inquirer rules were introduced in the first lesson of Term 1: do not re-teach them.

Plain statement for families when it comes up: counting coins and notes and change from $5 or $10 is Primary 1 work; listing every way to make an amount, the fewest notes and coins for $73 and how many different amounts three pieces can make go beyond Primary 1 on purpose, always with the play money in hand.

New here? Say in one minute: our three rule words (notice it, test it, explain why); a guess is fine and you can always pass; after Start here you may choose Think harder, Go further or the Investigation; nobody holds paper to the camera. A child without the play money uses small pieces of paper with a value written on each.
@rec
Count in fives with me. Clap on every ten. Five, ten, fifteen, twenty, all the way to one hundred.
Count in 5s to 100 together, clapping on every 10. Then count in 10s to 100.
Take these four coins from your kit: twenty cents, five cents, fifty cents and ten cents. Read the number on each coin. Put them in order, the least first.
Children put the four coins in order, least to most.
Which coin is worth the least? Which is worth the most?
What is the order, from least to most?
Count up from twenty-eight to thirty-five. Put a finger on the line and count the steps.
How many steps from twenty-eight to thirty-five?
From forty-six to fifty?
Change works the same way. We count up from the price to the money we paid.

If a child is unsure counting in 5s, count along the number row on the slide. For the coins, read the number on each coin out loud: the number is the value. For counting up, touch each tick on the line with a finger.
Answers: the 5s count to 100; 5, 10, 20, 50; 7 steps, 4 steps. Children answer with a whisper, fingers or hands. Nobody writes. Joining cold: all you need is counting to 20 and the picture.
@rec
Two sneak-peek puzzles: ideas we have not learnt yet. A guess is a great start, and I do not know is welcome. Nobody is marked.
Puzzle one. Count the coins: 3 ten-cent coins and 2 five-cent coins. How many cents? Write the number.
Children write the number on their own paper. Play money is fine to use.
Puzzle two. Mei has a one-dollar coin. Ben has 10 ten-cent coins. Does Mei have more money than Ben? Circle Yes or No. I know because blank.
Children write or draw their answer.
Keep your paper. Nobody shows it. We will check our own thinking later, at Talk time.

Puzzle 1 answer: 40 cents. Puzzle 2 answer: No, they have the same (10 tens make 100 cents and a dollar is 100 cents). Look for good ideas to praise later (a child who counted the tens first, or who said ten 10-cent coins is 100). Do not write scores or keep a list.
@rec
Today your play money is the teacher. Look at the number on each coin: that number is the value. A fifty-cent coin is worth fifty cents. Make sixty cents. Show me one way.
Children make 60 cents with their coins. Tutor scans the cameras and the tables.
Tell me one way you made sixty cents.
Now make sixty cents a different way. Same money, different coins.
Children make 60 cents a different way.
Who made it a different way? Tell us your coins.
Round two. Count the money in each picture. Start with the biggest coin, then count on.
Children count picture A, then picture B, aloud or with their own coins.
How many cents in picture A?
How many cents in picture B?
Round three. Change is the money the shop gives back. A sweet costs forty cents. You pay with a fifty-cent coin. Count up from forty cents to fifty cents. Put a coin down at each step.
Children count up from 40¢ to 50¢ with coins.
How much change did the shop give back?
Now a ruler costs six dollars. You pay with a ten-dollar note. Count up from six dollars to ten dollars with your two-dollar notes or your dollar tokens.
Children count up from $6 to $10 with notes or tokens.
How much change?

A child who counts each coin as 1: ask what number is on the coin. A child with only one way to make 60 cents: ask can you use only ten-cent coins? A child with too few coins uses paper pieces with a value written on each. For change, a child who gives the price back instead of the change: put the price coins away first, then count up.

Main room only; children say what they have made and may tilt the camera to the table. Answers: A is 70 cents, B is 65 cents; the sweet change is 10 cents, the ruler change is $4. Accept any right way to make 60 cents (50 and 10; 20, 20 and 20; six 10s; 20, 20, 10 and 10; and more). Do not say the rule before the children do.
@rec

Coins and notes. Coins are five, ten, twenty and fifty cents, and one dollar. Notes are two, five, ten and fifty dollars. We write cents with the cent sign after the number. We write dollars with the dollar sign before it. The number tells the value, not the size.
Which piece on the slide is worth the most?
Which is worth more, the five-dollar note or the fifty-cent coin?
Children find a ten-cent coin, a twenty-cent coin and a two-dollar note in their kit and touch each one as the tutor names it.
Count the biggest first. A fifty-cent coin, two ten-cent coins and a five-cent coin. Fifty. Then count on: sixty, seventy, seventy-five. Seventy-five cents.
Why do we start with the biggest coin?
The biggest coin gives us the biggest jump, and we do not lose count. Now you try with your coins: put down a twenty-cent coin, a twenty-cent coin and a ten-cent coin. Count the biggest first.
Children put down 20¢, 20¢ and 10¢ and count them.
How many cents?
One dollar is one hundred cents. Two fifty-cent coins make a dollar. Count in tens to a hundred on your fingers. You do not need ten coins.
Children put two 50¢ coins next to a $1 token, then count in tens to 100 on their fingers.
How many ten-cent coins make one dollar?
Change by counting up. The ball costs eight dollars. You pay with a ten-dollar note. Count up from eight dollars to ten dollars.
How much change do you get?
Two dollars. The price and the change make the money you paid.
Cents work the same way. A pencil costs thirty-five cents. You pay with a fifty-cent coin. Count up from thirty-five to fifty.
How many cents is the change?
Fifteen cents. Count up in tens and fives: forty-five, then fifty.
Your turn. Count a twenty-cent coin, a twenty-cent coin and a five-cent coin. Then find the change for a rubber that costs five dollars when you pay with a ten-dollar note. Write both answers.
Children write the two answers on their own paper. Wait 10 seconds before helping.
Forty-five cents. Five dollars. Tick your own work with a tick.

Key words to use every time: value, count on, change, count up, cents, dollars. Say fifty-cent coin or 50 cents, never 50c; and never say one dollar fifty. Do not teach decimal money. Do not use the words subtract or take away for change unless a child does.

If a child counts the coins in any order and gets lost, put the biggest coin first and count on. If a child thinks 50 cents is more than $1 because 50 is a bigger number, put two fifty-cent coins next to a $1 token. If a child gives the price as the change, ask: what do we count up to?
@rec
Stand up and get a sip of water. I call an amount. Hop once for every five cents and count out loud in fives. Twenty cents is four hops.
Call 20¢, 35¢, 50¢ and 10¢, then two amounts in a row. Children hop once for each 5¢ and count aloud in 5s; a child who sits taps the table.

Page 1, Start here. Question 1: count the money. How many cents? Question 2: count the notes. How many dollars? Question 3: look at the fifty-cent coin. It is worth the same as how many ten-cent coins? And how many five-cent coins?
Page 1, questions 1 to 3. Tutor walks the cameras, asks how do you know. Wait 10 seconds before helping.

After question 3 you may choose: carry on, or try Think harder. Everyone may choose, at any time.

When you have finished Start here, you can choose Think harder, Go further or the Investigation. Everyone may choose. You can swap at any time. Anything not finished is for home too.

Q1: biggest coin first, then count on. Q2: biggest note first. Q3: count the 10s up to 50, and the 5s up to 50. Q4: start with the 50¢ coin; what is left to make 55? Q5: is 1 dollar worth more or less than 2 dollars? Q6: count up from $3 to $5 with your play money.

A child who is still stuck ticks I am still stuck on the look-back page. The grown-up can photograph that page after class and send it to the business WhatsApp (never a personal phone). You then help in the open session in the next lesson. Never a private message to a child.

Think harder has two things and change, a dollar in cents, all the ways to make 50 cents, and sets of coins. Start here takes a middle child about 17 minutes, so the choice time is short: for most children pages 3 to 5 are for home. Say so plainly, do not skip the answer slides, and take any extra minutes from the flex time.

A child says: a fifty-cent coin is worth more than a one-dollar coin. Is the child right? How could we check with our coins?
Test it with your coins: put a one-dollar token next to two fifty-cent coins.
Talk to the grown-up next to you or to your screen for one minute. Use the sentence starter: I think... because...
Who would like to share? Volunteers first. A pass is always fine.
Remember the sneak-peek? Puzzle one: forty cents. Puzzle two: ten ten-cent coins make one hundred cents, and a one-dollar coin is one hundred cents. They have the same.
Did anyone change their mind while we worked? You can just nod.

Model answer: no. A one-dollar coin is 100 cents and a fifty-cent coin is half of that. Two fifty-cent coins make one dollar. 50 is a bigger number than 1, but cents are smaller than dollars. start.text: Count the money. Fill in the blank.
start.hint: Start with the biggest coin. Count on: 50, then 70, then 75, then 80.
start.solution: The coins are 50¢, 20¢, 5¢ and 5¢. 50 and 20 make 70. 70 and 5 make 75. 75 and 5 make 80. The total is 80¢.
mistakes: Writing 4 (counting the coins).
Writing 75 (leaving out the last 5¢ coin).

start.text: Count the notes. Fill in the blank.
start.hint: Start with the biggest note. Count on in dollars.
start.solution: The notes are $10, $5, $2 and $2. 10 and 5 make 15. 15 and 2 make 17. 17 and 2 make 19. The total is $19.
mistakes: Writing 4 (counting the notes).
Writing $17 (leaving out one $2 note).

start.text: Look at the fifty-cent coin. Count in 10s, then in 5s.

parts.text: It is worth the same as ____ ten-cent coins.
It is worth the same as ____ five-cent coins.

start.hint: Count in 10s to 50. Then count in 5s to 50.
start.solution: Five 10¢ coins make 50¢: 10, 20, 30, 40, 50. Ten 5¢ coins make 50¢: 5, 10, 15, up to 50.
mistakes: Writing 50 or 1 (the coin itself).
Writing 5 for the five-cent coins (the same as the ten-cent answer).

parts.text: I circled the ____¢ coin and the ____¢ coin.

start.hint: Start with the biggest coin that fits. What is left to make 55?
start.solution: The 50¢ coin and one 5¢ coin make 55¢. 50 and 5 make 55. Either 5¢ coin may be circled. The two blanks may be filled in either order.
mistakes: Circling the 20¢ coin first (it leaves 35¢ and the coins that are left cannot make it).
Circling every coin.

start.text: Look at the two pieces of money.

parts.text: Which is worth more? Circle one.

start.hint: 2 dollars and 1 dollar. Which number is greater?
start.solution: A two-dollar note is worth $2. A one-dollar coin is worth $1. 2 is greater than 1, so the $2 note is worth more.
mistakes: Circling the $1 coin because it is a coin (the value is the number on the piece, not its shape).
Thinking they are worth the same.

start.text: Ravi buys a toy car for $3. He pays with a five-dollar note. How much change does he get?
start.solution: Count up from $3 to $5: $4, $5. That is 2 dollars. The change is $2. Check: 3 and 2 make 5.
mistakes: Writing $5 (the note) or $3 (the price).
Writing $8 (adding).

think.text: A ruler costs $4. A book costs $5. Mei pays with a ten-dollar note.
think.hint: First find how much the two things cost together.
think.solution: 4 and 5 make 9, so the two things cost $9 together. Count up from $9 to $10: the change is $1. Check: 9 and 1 make 10.
mistakes: Writing $1 for the cost (giving the change first).
Writing $6 (10 minus 4).

think.text: Ali makes 50¢ with ten-cent coins and twenty-cent coins. One way is shown. Find the other 2 ways.
think.hint: Try 1 twenty-cent coin. How much is left to make with ten-cent coins?
think.solution: Five 10¢ coins make 50¢ (shown). With one 20¢ coin, 30¢ is left, which is three 10¢ coins. With two 20¢ coins, 10¢ is left, which is one 10¢ coin. The two ways are 3 and 1, and 1 and 2, in either order.
mistakes: Writing a way that makes more or less than 50¢.
Using three 20¢ coins (60¢ is too much).

think.text: Siti buys a pencil. She pays with a one-dollar coin and gets 40¢ change.
think.hint: A one-dollar coin is worth 100¢. The price and the change make 100¢. Count back 40 from 100.
think.solution: A one-dollar coin is worth 100¢. The price and the change together make the 100¢ she paid. Count back 40 from 100 in 10s: 90, 80, 70, 60. The pencil costs 60¢. Check: count up from 60¢ to 100¢ and you get 40¢ change.
mistakes: Writing 40¢ (the change) for the price.
Writing 140¢ (adding the change to the coin).

think.text: Look at the three sets of coins.

parts.text: Which set has the most money? Circle one.
Set A is worth ____¢ more than Set C.

think.hint: Count each set, biggest coin first. Do not count the coins.
think.solution: Set A is 50, 70, 80: 80¢. Set B is 20, 40, 60, 70: 70¢. Set C is 50, 55, 60: 60¢. Set A has the most money, even though Set B has the most coins. Set A has 20¢ more than Set C: 80 minus 60.
mistakes: Circling Set B because it has the most coins.
Writing 80¢ or 3¢ for the difference.

go.text: Use these notes and coins. You may use each one as many times as you like.

parts.text: The fewest notes and coins that make $73 is ____ pieces.
Kumar pays with a $50 note for a toy that costs $37. His change in the fewest notes and coins is ____ pieces.

go.hint: Take the biggest note that fits first. Then the next biggest.
go.solution: $73: $50 leaves $23; $10 and $10 leave $3; $2 and $1 leave nothing. That is $50, $10, $10, $2 and $1, which is 5 pieces. $50 minus $37 is $13: $10, $2 and $1, which is 3 pieces.
mistakes: Writing 9 (seven $10 notes, a $2 note and a $1 coin, without the $50 note).
Using a $20 note (there is no $20 note).

go.text: Mei has a $5 note, a $2 note and a $1 coin. She uses one, two or all three pieces.
go.hint: Start with one piece at a time. Then try two pieces together.
go.solution: One piece: $1, $2, $5. Two pieces: $1 and $2 make $3, $1 and $5 make $6, $2 and $5 make $7. All three: $8. That is 7 different amounts: $1, $2, $3, $5, $6, $7, $8.
mistakes: Writing 3 (only one piece at a time).
Forgetting the three-piece amount, $8, or writing $4 (which cannot be made).

go.text: A sticker costs 30¢. Ben has a one-dollar coin.
go.hint: A one-dollar coin is 100¢. Count in 30s: 30, 60, 90. Will 120 fit?
go.solution: 30, 60 and 90 are three stickers, 90¢. Four stickers would cost 120¢, which is more than 100¢. Ben buys 3 stickers. Count up from 90¢ to 100¢: the change is 10¢.
mistakes: Writing 4 (120¢ is more than he has).
Writing 70¢ (100 minus 30, for one sticker).

investigation.title: Coin detective
investigation.first: Make 35¢ with any coins. Write them.
investigation.text: Make 35¢ with exactly 3 coins. Then with exactly 4 coins. Find every way.
investigation.answer: First: any way that makes 35¢, for example 20¢, 10¢ and 5¢. Exactly 3 coins: one way only, 20¢, 10¢ and 5¢. Exactly 4 coins: two ways, 10¢, 10¢, 10¢ and 5¢; or 20¢, 5¢, 5¢ and 5¢. Two coins cannot make 35¢.
investigation.look_for: A child who tries a big coin first and then fills in the rest; a child who checks each way by counting back to 35; a child who finds the second 4-coin way by swapping a 20¢ coin for ten and ten, or three 5s. Credit any clear reason. Do not mark a child down for stopping at one way.
mistakes: A way with the wrong total.
Using a coin more times than there are in the kit (the kit has four 5¢ coins).

talk.question: A child says: a fifty-cent coin is worth more than a one-dollar coin. Is the child right? How could we check with our coins?
talk.answer: No. A one-dollar coin is 100 cents. A fifty-cent coin is 50 cents, which is half of a dollar. Two fifty-cent coins make one dollar. We can check by putting two fifty-cent coins next to a one-dollar coin.
talk.look_for: A child who tests it with the coins, or says a dollar is 100 cents, or says two fifty-cent coins make a dollar. Not just yes or no.

exit.text: Count the money. Fill in the blank.
exit.solution: The coins are 50¢, 20¢, 10¢ and 10¢. 50 and 20 make 70. 70 and 10 make 80. 80 and 10 make 90. The total is 90¢.
mistakes: Writing 4 (counting the coins).
Writing 80 (leaving out one 10¢ coin).

exit.text: Mei pays $10 for a pen that costs $4. How much change does she get? Choose the correct answer. Write its number in the bracket.
exit.solution: Count up from $4 to $10: $5, $6, $7, $8, $9, $10. That is 6 dollars. The change is $6. Check: 4 and 6 make 10.
mistakes: Choosing (1) $4, the price.
Choosing (4) $14, which adds the price and the note.

exit.text: Ali has a $10 note, two $2 notes and one $1 coin. How much money does he have?
exit.solution: Start with the biggest: $10. Two $2 notes make $4, so 10 and 4 make $14. Add the $1 coin: $15.
mistakes: Writing $14 (leaving out the $1 coin).
Writing 4 (counting the pieces).

home_practice.text: Ali has two 20¢ coins, a 10¢ coin and a 5¢ coin. How much does he have in all? ____¢
home_practice.solution: Start with the biggest: 20 and 20 make 40. 40 and 10 make 50. 50 and 5 make 55. He has 55¢.

home_practice.text: A bun costs $2. Siti pays with a five-dollar note. How much change does she get? $____
home_practice.solution: Count up from $2 to $5: $3, $4, $5. That is 3 dollars. The change is $3.

home_practice.text: Ben buys a sandwich for $3 and a drink for $2. He pays with a ten-dollar note. How much change does he get? $____
home_practice.solution: 3 and 2 make 5, so the two things cost $5. Count up from $5 to $10: the change is $5.

home_practice.text: What is the fewest number of notes and coins that make $46? There is no $20 note. ____ pieces
home_practice.solution: Take the biggest piece that fits each time: $10, $10, $10 and $10 make $40. Then $5 and $1 make $6. That is 4 + 2 = 6 pieces.

home_practice.text: Count in 5s. Write the next three numbers: 40, 45, 50, ___, ___, ___.

items.q: Count the coins. How many cents is that? Write the number.
items.hint: Start with the biggest coin. Count on.

slips.say: 3 is how many coins there are. Count the value of each coin.

tpl.q: Count the coins. How many cents is that? Write the number.
tpl.hint: Start with the biggest coin. Count on.
steps: The coins are {a} twenty-cent, {b} ten-cent and {c} five-cent.
Count the biggest first, then count on.

items.q: Count the notes. How many dollars is that? Write the number.
items.hint: Start with the biggest note. Count on in dollars.

slips.say: 3 is how many notes there are. Add the value of each note.

tpl.q: Count the notes. How many dollars is that? Write the number.
tpl.hint: Start with the biggest note. Count on in dollars.
steps: The notes are {a} ten-dollar, {b} five-dollar and {c} two-dollar.
Count the biggest first, then count on.

items.q: A ball costs $3. You pay with a $5 note. How many dollars is your change?
items.hint: Count up from the price to the money you paid.

slips.say: 5 is the money you paid. The change is what the shop gives back.
Do not add. Count up from the price to the money you paid.

tpl.q: A ball costs ${p}. You pay with a $5 note. How many dollars is your change?
tpl.hint: Count up from the price to the money you paid.

items.q: A book costs $6. You pay with a $10 note. How many dollars is your change?
items.hint: Count up from the price to the money you paid.

slips.say: 10 is the money you paid. The change is what the shop gives back.
Do not add. Count up from the price to the money you paid.

tpl.q: A book costs ${p}. You pay with a $10 note. How many dollars is your change?
tpl.hint: Count up from the price to the money you paid.

items.q: Which is worth more, a $2 note or a $1 coin?
steps: 2 is greater than 1, so the $2 note is worth more.

slips.say: The value is the number on the piece, not its size.

items.q: A pencil costs 60¢. You pay with a $1 coin. How many cents is your change?
items.hint: A $1 coin is worth 100¢. Count up from the price to 100¢.
steps: Count up from 60¢ to 100¢: that is 40¢.

slips.say: 60 is the price. The change is what the shop gives back.
Do not add. Count up from the price to 100.

tpl.q: A pencil costs {p}¢. You pay with a $1 coin. How many cents is your change?
tpl.hint: A $1 coin is worth 100¢. Count up from the price to 100¢.
steps: Count up from {p}¢ to 100¢: that is {t}¢.

items.q: A ruler costs $4. A book costs $5. You pay with a $10 note. How many dollars is your change?
items.hint: Find the cost of both things first.
steps: 4 and 5 make 9, so the two things cost $9.
Count up from $9 to $10: that is 1 dollar.

slips.say: 9 is how much the two things cost. The change is what the shop gives back.
That is 10 minus 4 only. Add the book as well.

tpl.q: A ruler costs ${a}. A book costs ${b}. You pay with a $10 note. How many dollars is your change?
tpl.hint: Find the cost of both things first.
steps: {a} and {b} make {s}, so the two things cost ${s}.
Count up from ${s} to $10: that is {t} dollars.

items.q: Make 50¢ with one 20¢ coin and some 10¢ coins. How many 10¢ coins do you need?
items.hint: One 20¢ coin leaves 30¢ to make with ten-cent coins.
steps: 50 minus 20 is 30, which is three 10¢ coins.

slips.say: One 20¢ coin and two 10¢ coins make only 40¢. Count up to 50¢.
Five 10¢ coins make 50¢ on their own. This way there is a 20¢ coin too.

items.q: What is the fewest number of notes and coins that make $73? Use $1, $2, $5, $10 and $50.
items.hint: Take the biggest piece that fits first.

slips.say: Try a bigger piece first. A $50 note covers most of $73.

tpl.q: What is the fewest number of notes and coins that make ${n}? Use $1, $2, $5, $10 and $50.
tpl.hint: Take the biggest piece that fits first.
steps: Take the biggest piece that fits, then the next biggest, until nothing is left.

items.q: Mei has a $5 note, a $2 note and a $1 coin. She uses one, two or all three pieces. How many different amounts can she make?
items.hint: List the amounts with one piece, then two pieces, then all three.

slips.say: 3 is only the amounts with one piece. Try two pieces together, and all three.
8 is the most money she can make. How many different amounts are there?

items.q: Make a shop puzzle for a grown-up. Choose a price and a note. Ask how much change. Check the answer with your play money.
items.hint: Pick the price first, then the note.
steps: Choose a price and a note that is worth more.
Count up from the price to the note with your play money.
Ask a grown-up, then check together.

spare_time.note: Optional time, never added to the 90-minute sum. It comes from the 5-minute flex buffer, from slack in the parts, or from the optional Go further slide.
rules: Whole class ahead: use the Spare-time menu in the Flex time and the optional Go further slide. Pick one or two activities; do not start new content.
A few children ahead: they may choose Go further or the Investigation, which are open to everyone. Never label or name a child, and never announce who is ahead.
Never teach anything the next lesson needs. If the class is ahead, slow down: ask 'How do you know?' and let children explain, rather than rushing on.

menu.title: Is it always true?
menu.tutor: Mei says: the more coins you have, the more money you have. Is that always true? Test it: a fifty-cent coin against four five-cent coins.
menu.rec: Recording: pause. Mei says more coins always means more money. Test one 50 cent coin against four 5 cent coins.
menu.answer: No. Four 5-cent coins are worth 20 cents, and one 50-cent coin is worth 50 cents. What matters is the value of each coin, not how many coins there are.

menu.title: Make a puzzle for your grown-up
menu.tutor: Pick 3 coins from your kit. Add them up in your head. Tell your grown-up the total and ask: which 3 coins are they? Check with the coins.
menu.rec: Recording: pause. Pick 3 coins. Tell a grown-up the total and ask which coins they are.
menu.answer: No single answer. For example 20¢, 10¢ and 5¢ make 35¢, and 35¢ can only be made from 3 of these coins in that one way.

menu.title: Teach it back
menu.tutor: Pretend your grown-up or a toy has never given change. Teach them how to count up from a price of 6 dollars to a 10-dollar note.
menu.rec: Recording: pause. Teach a grown-up how to count up for change from $6 to $10.
menu.answer: Start at the price, $6, and count up in dollars: $7, $8, $9, $10. That is 4 steps, so the change is $4. The price and the change make the money you paid.

parent.summary: We worked with play money. Your child named coins and notes by value, counted mixed coins and notes, biggest first, made 60 cents in different ways, and found change by counting up from the price to the money paid. Counting coins and notes and change from $5 or $10 is Primary 1 work.
words: value: how much a coin or note is worth
change: the money the shop gives back
count up: start at the price and count on to the money paid
try_home: Purse game: put some play money on the table (real coins only with a grown-up beside you; small coins stay on the table, away from little ones). Count them together, biggest first. Ask: how do you know?
Shop game: pick a price and pay with a note. Count up together for the change.
Two ways: ask your child to show 50¢ in two different ways with coins.
ask: What is the number on the coin?
Which coin do you count first?
How did you find the change?
parent.when_stuck: Let your child use the play money and wait 10 seconds before helping. Asking 'what do we count up to?' works better than giving the answer. Please do not teach decimal money such as $1.50: we write cents and dollars apart. If the look-back page says 'I am still stuck', photograph it and send it to our business WhatsApp (+65 9880 5962). Photos are kept 90 days after the program ends.
parent.next: Next lesson: Price Tags: Compare and Choose. Online practice: your tutor will share the link. The recording has the tutor, the shared screen and any voice that is not muted; your child may mute and keep the camera off. The recording link is private to your family: please do not share it.
parent.quote: Count the biggest first. Change is what we count up from the price to the money we paid.
parent.report_line: Your child is learning to count coins and notes, to make an amount in different ways and to find change by counting up. This week: counting money, and change from $5 and $10.
parent.term_line: Your child is learning to give a reason, and to read time and money in real life.
next_materials: The price-tag page, cut out by a grown-up (12 tags)
Your play money and the $1 tokens, kept in the envelope

safeguarding: The play money is small: it stays on the table, nothing goes in the mouth or ears, and it is kept away from younger brothers and sisters. It is play money, not real money. Real coins only if a grown-up is present. No matches, toothpicks or anything sharp. Nobody cuts during the lesson; a grown-up cuts the pieces beforehand.
This lesson uses the main room only: no breakout rooms, so the tutor sees every camera. A parent sits nearby but does not give answers.

Nobody holds paper or a board up to the camera: a gallery view shows everyone. Children tick their own work against the answer slide, answer together on a count of three, or show fingers or a thumb for a choice. There is no private chat.

Never read out a child's name with a right or wrong answer. The recording has the tutor, the shared screen and any voice that is unmuted. Children may mute and keep their cameras off. A child's page is never shown.
Movement break: children need a little clear space, soft shoes or socks on a safe floor, no stairs and no running. Hopping is quiet and small; a child may stay seated and tap the table.

A child who is still stuck ticks 'I am still stuck' on the look-back page. A grown-up may photograph that page after class and send it to the business WhatsApp only; photos are kept for 90 days after the program ends. The tutor then helps in the open session next lesson. No private messages to children, and no personal phones.
The look-back is never collected in front of the group or read out. A pass is always allowed.
tutor_prep: Solve every workbook question yourself first, with your own play money. Check: S1 80¢; S2 $19; S3 5 and 10; S4 50¢ and 5¢ (the 50¢ coin and one 5¢ coin); S5 the $2 note; S6 $2; T1 $9 and $1; T2 3 and 1, 1 and 2; T3 100¢ and 60¢; T4 Set A and 20¢; G1 5 and 3; G2 7 amounts; G3 3 stickers and 10¢.

Tell parents a week before: this is the heaviest cutting of the term. Tear out the two play-money pages (pages 6 and 7) along the dashed line; a grown-up cuts out all 29 pieces (16 coins and 13 notes) and keeps them in an envelope. The $1 coins are the tokens from Term 2 Lesson 10; with no tokens use 5 counters or buttons. Print on card if you can; paper scraps with a value written on them also work.
Have the slides open. Have your own play money to show on camera if you wish. Say each amount both ways, never 50c: fifty-cent coin or 50¢; five-dollar note or $5. Never write or say $1.50.

Check the recording captures the tutor and the shared screen. Children video is excluded; any unmuted voice is recorded. Greet the whole group warmly, then start the recording, then say the notice; do not use children's first names on the recording.

Be plain with families: counting coins and notes and change from $5 or $10 is Primary 1 work; listing every way, the fewest notes and coins for $73 and how many different amounts three pieces can make are beyond Primary 1 on purpose. Do not call the lesson MOE-aligned. The money is PLAY MONEY, stylised and not a copy of any real note or coin.

Slides s-m3, s-m4 and s-m5 keep the answers off the screen while you ask: the answer slide follows. The money on the workbook slides is shown large, but say each amount aloud too, and read the four options of E2 aloud. Children say what they have made and may tilt the camera to the table, not the room.

kits.title: Kit page: play money, coins
kits.intro: A grown-up cuts out all 16 coins before the lesson: 4 five-cent, 6 ten-cent, 4 twenty-cent and 2 fifty-cent coins. This is play money, not real money. The $1 coins are the tokens from Term 2 Lesson 10. Keep all the money in an envelope: we use it in the next two lessons and in the Quest.

kits.title: Kit page: play money, notes
kits.intro: A grown-up cuts out all 13 notes before the lesson: 5 two-dollar, 4 five-dollar, 3 ten-dollar and 1 fifty-dollar note. This is play money, not real money. There is no twenty-dollar note. Keep it in the envelope with the coins.

beyond.name: Fewest Notes and Coins
beyond.text: The fewest notes and coins for $73 and for a change of $13, and how many different amounts a $5 note, a $2 note and a $1 coin can make. School papers set the fewest-pieces question for smaller amounts ($17, $43), so only the size and the notes $10 and $50 are the stretch; listing every amount is not a syllabus item. Named puzzle: Fewest Notes and Coins. T2 (every way to make 50¢ with 10¢ and 20¢ coins) is a listing puzzle too.
beyond.parent: Listing every way to make an amount, how many different amounts three pieces can make, and the fewest notes and coins for $73 go past the school Primary 1 syllabus on purpose.
